hero.description: Phou Si works best as an orientation climb: 328 steps rise from the centre of Luang Prabang to a sacred summit where the Mekong, Nam Khan, old-town roofs and surrounding hills finally line up in one view.
steps: Pause at religious stops on the way
Use the summit to read both rivers

chapters.label: THE CLIMB
chapters.title: This is a sacred hill before it is a viewpoint
chapters.body: Phou Si rises directly out of the historic centre and the official tourism office treats the summit as a religious site as well as a panorama. The climb passes temple structures and devotional spaces, so take the stairs steadily and keep the same dress and behaviour you would use in a monastery compound.

chapters.label: THE VIEW
chapters.title: The summit explains the town in one glance
chapters.body: From above, Luang Prabang’s narrow urban shape becomes obvious: old-town roofs sit between the Mekong and Nam Khan while hills close the horizon beyond. That makes Phou Si especially useful early in a stay, when the geography is still abstract at street level.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: Choose sunset for atmosphere; choose morning or earlier afternoon for more space and a cleaner sense of the town.

items.label: Climb
items.detail: There are four official access points around the hill, so you do not have to descend the same way you came up.

items.label: Time
items.detail: Enough for the stairs, intermediate stops and a real pause at the summit.

items.label: Best time
items.detail: Sunset is the classic choice but also draws the largest concentration of visitors.

items.label: Respect
items.detail: Dress appropriately and follow temple behaviour; alcohol is prohibited on the summit according to the official tourism office.

faq.question: How difficult is the Phou Si climb?
faq.answer: It is a stair climb rather than a hike. The main approach has 328 steps, so most visitors can manage it comfortably with steady pauses.

faq.question: Is sunset worth it?
faq.answer: Yes if you want the classic atmosphere, but it is also the busiest time. Morning or earlier afternoon is better if space matters more than sunset colour.

faq.question: Are there different ways up?
faq.answer: Yes. The official tourism office lists four access points around Phou Si, which makes it possible to climb one side and descend another.

faq.question: How long should I allow?
faq.answer: Plan one to two hours including the climb, temple stops and time at the summit.

faq.question: Is Phou Si only a viewpoint?
faq.answer: No. It is a sacred religious site with temples and long-standing local traditions, so treat the hill accordingly.
